sources.title: NPR Topics: Home Page Top Stories

articles.author: The Associated Press
articles.description: The National Hurricane Center said late Wednesday that the hurricane was on track to strike the U.S. Gulf Coast later in the week. It's expected to bring heavy rains and potentially flash flooding.
articles.title: Isaias strengthens into the first hurricane of the Atlantic season

articles.author: Michaeleen Doucleff
articles.description: The ancient disease of plague is back in the headlines after the death this month of a Russian lab worker.
articles.title: What is the pneumonic plague?

articles.author: Laura Kwerel
articles.description: A 7-year-old girl was injured riding her new bike. A stranger came to her rescue and gifted her an origami crane with a hidden message she would only discover years later.
articles.title: A childhood bike crash led to a stranger's gift — and a hidden message

articles.author: Ari Daniel
articles.description: It's likely you've already chewed and swallowed some tasty morsel today. But when did that ability emerge? New evidence points to at least the middle Jurassic, back when dinosaurs still reigned.
articles.title: This surprising mammal fossil is giving scientists something to chew on

articles.author: Scott Neuman
articles.description: A week after the failed execution, Pike is awake but is said to be angry and confused. Her lawyers said Wednesday's hearing was about "transparency."
articles.title: Judge orders that Christa Pike execution evidence be preserved

articles.author: Rachel Treisman
articles.description: The Pentagon says Nidal Hasan will be executed by firing squad in December at Fort Hood, where he killed 13 people in 2009. The announcement came days after a botched lethal injection in Tennessee.
articles.title: Trump approved the military's 1st firing squad execution since WWII. Why now?

articles.author: Willa Rubin
articles.description: Trump is temporarily allowing this fuel to be used on highways, although it's typically just for off-road farm and construction vehicles. Could that lower the price of diesel?
articles.title: Why Trump just loosened the rules on 'dyed diesel' — normally a farm fuel

articles.author: Selena Simmons-Duffin
articles.description: As checks from President Trump for health costs hit millions of mailboxes, a poll shows Americans don't trust Republicans on healthcare. Experts doubt it will move the needle and say it is likely illegal.
articles.title: She got Trump's $500 check for health insurance. To her, it's a 'political stunt'

articles.author: Pien Huang
articles.description: New research looks at the surprising similarities in the gut microbiomes of hunter-gathers in Tanzania and horticulturalists in Bolivia, and asks: What role do these bacteria play in human health?
articles.title: Gut microbes followed migrating humans across continents, new study suggests

articles.author: Diaa Hadid
articles.description: The Lahore High Court is a near-perfect specimen of British South Asian colonial architecture and its main square is a pleasant spot shaded by banyan trees.
articles.title: Greetings from Lahore, Pakistan, whose high court offers an oasis for chatter and chai

articles.author: Penry Buckley and Jordyn Beazley
articles.description:
Police watchdog says Mal Lanyon’s timing in raising the issue was ‘regrettable’ and led to delays

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

The New South Wales police commissioner made a last-minute bid to hold hearings into Sydney’s anti-Herzog protest behind closed doors, delaying the inquiry, the police watchdog has revealed.
The Law Enforcement Conduct Commission (Lecc) has said that its inquiry into the February protest at Sydney’s town hall, launched after widespread allegations of police brutality, would go ahead this month with a mix of public and private examinations, saying the timing of issues raised by police commissioner, Mal Lanyon, was “regrettable”.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: NSW police commissioner made last-minute bid to hold closed-door hearings into Sydney anti-Herzog protest

articles.author: Jillian Ambrose Energy correspondent
articles.description:
Move expected to make pump pricing more transparent and encourage competition after diesel hits record £2 a litre
Drivers will be able to see live petrol prices on Google Maps for the first time from Thursday, in a move that will help motorists shop around for the cheapest fuel.
Millions of motorists will be able to find the cheapest petrol and diesel prices by searching for a local forecourt in the Google app, in what could prove to be “a major development” in making fuel prices more fair, according to campaigners.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: UK motorists can now see live fuel prices on Google Maps

articles.author: Ben Quinn with photographs by Graeme Robertson
articles.description:
Little if any sign Bury Park is a place where any group might fear to tread, despite Tory MP’s comments to the contrary
From behind the counter of his chippie, Tanner Ahmed is wrestling with the notion that the regular stop-off point for fans attending Luton Town’s nearby football ground could be in a “no-go zone” for white people.
“The whole point of setting up was to cater for thousands who were coming through here every week, especially in the first year when the club was in the Premier League,” said Ahmed, affectionately known as Mr T, in the Bury Park area, a predominantly Asian district of Luton.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘I feel perfectly safe’: white Lutonians on the town’s supposed no-go zones

articles.author: Amanda Meade
articles.description:
Youngest complainant in trial alleges Jones put his tongue in his mouth and touched him on the bottom during visit to shock jock’s property

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Listen to the podcast Alan Jones on Trial

An alleged teenage victim of Alan Jones has denied his family tried to deceive the broadcaster and get as much money out of him as they could during a tense cross-examination in a Sydney court.
Asked whether he was intent on getting as much financial assistance as he could from the former 2GB host, the witness replied: “That is a lie.”
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘That is a lie’: alleged Alan Jones victim denies family tried to get money out of broadcaster, court hears

articles.author: Raphael Rashid in Seoul
articles.description:
Responding to a Guardian report that revealed thousands of tonnes of fuel was transported to Russia, Seoul said it was investigating the cases
South Korea will take legal action if it finds that shipments of fuel from its ports to Russia broke domestic law, the government has said, responding to a Guardian report on the trade.
The government, in a statement issued by the foreign and trade ministries and the customs service, said that it is “checking additional information concerning the loading cases reported by the Guardian” and “if the verification establishes that our laws and regulations have been violated, it plans to act in accordance with the law”.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: South Korea threatens legal action if fuel shipments to Russia found to have broken law

articles.author: Australian Associated Press
articles.description:
Former NSW police officer has pleaded not guilty to the February 2024 murders of Jesse Baird and Luke Davies in Sydney

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Marks made by a gun at close proximity were found on Jesse Baird after his decomposing body was discovered, a jury has heard.
Former police officer Beau Lamarre-Condon has pleaded not guilty to the February 2024 murders of Baird, his ex-partner, and the TV presenter’s new partner, Luke Davies.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Jurors in Beau Lamarre-Condon murder trial shown photo of alleged ‘execution-style’ gunshot wound

articles.author: Andrew Gregory Health editor
articles.description:
Operation on 19-year-old who had no sperm after chemotherapy offers hope of preserving children’s fertility after cancer treatment 
Surgeons have performed the first testicular tissue transplant on a teenager in the UK, offering hope that boys left infertile by chemotherapy could one day have biological children.
The 19-year-old had his tissue removed and frozen three years ago before undergoing treatment for a serious blood disorder. He said he was “incredibly grateful” to the medical team behind the pioneering procedure, which represents a potential breakthrough for male fertility preservation.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Teenager becomes first person to have testicular tissue transplant in UK

articles.author: Angela Giuffrida in Rome
articles.description:
In Bolotana, 70 miles from island’s original blue zone, 13% of women who reach 70 will live on to a century
The secret to longevity is being a woman – specifically, a woman in one part of Sardinia. At least, that is the conclusion of a study on centenarians in a tiny mountain village on the Italian island.
Sardinia became known as a haven for longevity, especially for long-lived men, in 1999 when a cluster of remote villages nestled in the slopes of its central and eastern provinces were classified among the world’s five “blue zones” – geographic areas with high concentrations of centenarians.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Sardinian village where more women reach 100 may be new centenarian ‘blue zone’

articles.author: Justin McCurry in Tokyo
articles.description:
Investigators probe Asahi, Kirin, Suntory and Sapporo breweries – which together control more than 90% of Japan’s beer market
Japanese authorities have raided the country’s four biggest breweries over suspicions they colluded to set the price of beer and other beverages – a practice media reports said could have forced drinkers to pay over the odds.
Officials from the Fair Trade Commission this week searched the offices of Asahi Breweries, Kirin Brewery, Suntory Beer and Sapporo Breweries – which together control more than 90% of the domestic market. The quartet are suspected of violating the anti-monopoly law.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Japan beer giants raided over suspicions they colluded to set the price of beverages

articles.author: Oliver Holmes in Bangkok and agencies
articles.description:
NGOs in Indonesian Borneo file class action lawsuit calling for government to better manage annual fires and 
The Indonesian government has been accused of “gross negligence” in a class action lawsuit over its handling of wildfires that have cloaked large parts of South-east Asia in a toxic haze, shuttered schools and caused a spike in respiratory illnesses.
The lawsuit, filed by indigenous and civil society groups in the Indonesian part of Borneo, named President Prabowo Subianto and the governor of West Kalimantan among 10 defendants. The case seeks comprehensive recovery and rehabilitation measures that would include covering the healthcare costs of residents.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Indonesia accused of ‘gross negligence’ in wildfires lawsuit as haze tests region

articles.author: David Smith in Washington
articles.description:
Trump briefly stepped away from the microphone after one protester appeared to approach the stage
Donald Trump’s latest campaign rally was rocked by repeated protests on Wednesday as the US president urged Texas voters to back embattled Senate candidate Ken Paxton.
At least half a dozen demonstrators interrupted the US president during his remarks in San Antonio, with some led away by police. One was physically assaulted by an older Trump supporter as he tried to leave the arena.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Donald Trump’s Texas rally rocked by repeated protests

articles.author: Robert Mackey, Shrai Popat, Marina Dunbar and Tom Ambrose
articles.description:
This live blog is now closed.

Sign up for the Breaking News US email

Tonight, we’ll have another set of midterm debates. In Iowa, we’ll see the Republican nominee for US Senate, Ashley Hinson, face off against Democrat Josh Turek, a state representative and Paralympian at 8pm ET.
The race has become one of the most competitive of this cycle, despite the fact a Democrat hasn’t won a Senate election in the Hawkeye state since 2008. Turek, however, trails by just a point in a recent New York Times/Siena College poll. And Hinson, who currently serves as a congresswoman, has pushed back on Donald Trump’s agenda of late, as the president’s approval rating sinks to a new low. Hinson has called for an end on the war in Iran, despite consistently voting against House war powers resolutions that would curb military action, and criticizing the president’s recent pause on tariffs for foreign beef imports, which, Hinson argues, will affect the bottom line for the many cattle ranchers in Iowa.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Trump repeats his false claim that Iran could destroy Los Angeles or San Diego – as it happened

articles.author: Josh Butler
articles.description:
Exclusive: Revelation comes after executive told parliamentary inquiry he did not believe AI had been used to write message, but was ‘happy to go and confirm’

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

OpenAI used AI to help write the email to the Australian government advising that its AI agent had hacked into key departmental websites, Guardian Australia can reveal.
On Tuesday, one of the company’s executives told a parliamentary inquiry that he didn’t believe that its own technology had been used to create the email, but said the company needed to confirm this.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: OpenAI used AI to help write email warning Australian government AI had hacked its websites

articles.author: Uwa Ede-Osifo
articles.description:
Jamaal Howard, 46, executed by fatal dose of pentobarbital after lawyers’ bid for stay had been denied
A Texas man was put to death Wednesday in the first US execution since the botched lethal injection of Christa Pike in Tennessee last week.
Jamaal Howard, 46, was pronounced dead at 8.03pm after receiving a fatal dose of pentobarbital, a sedative, at the state prison in Huntsville.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Texas kills man in first US execution since botched lethal injection of Christa Pike

articles.author: Jonathan Barrett
articles.description:
Sources say Firmus is slashing its price and may even shelve initial public offering altogether

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

The momentum behind Firmus Technologies’ high-flying valuation is showing severe cracks just weeks out from its anticipated ASX debut.
Multiple sources briefed on the matter told Guardian Australia the AI datacentre company is slashing its valuation to entice sceptical investors – or may even shelve its initial public offering altogether.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Datacentre company Firmus’s high flying valuation may be coming back down to earth ahead of expected ASX debut

articles.author: Uwa Ede-Osifo
articles.description:
MIT computer scientist led development of software for moon mission and earned Presidential Medal of Freedom
Margaret Hamilton, the computer pioneer whose software powered the first moon landing, has died, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) announced on Wednesday. She was 90.
In an era before titles such as software engineer and computer scientist became mainstream, Hamilton, who died on 30 September, learned to program under the tutelage of a renowned MIT meteorologist.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Margaret Hamilton, trailblazer whose software powered Apollo 11 moon landing, dies at 90

articles.author: Sam Levin in Los Angeles
articles.description:
The 78-year-old has spent nearly six decades in prison and California governor has overturned last two parole grants
Patricia Krenwinkel, a former Charles Manson follower, was granted parole on Tuesday after nearly six decades in prison for her role in the infamous Tate-LaBianca murders in Los Angeles.
This is the third time that Krenwinkel, 78, has been approved for release by California’s board of parole hearings. After both of her last two parole grants, Gavin Newsom, California’s governor, reversed the parole board’s decisions and denied her freedom, and Krenwinkel’s attorneys are now urging the Democrat to allow this latest ruling to stand.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Patricia Krenwinkel, former Manson follower, granted parole for third time

articles.author: Pippa Neill Environment reporter
articles.description:
Hundred-and-fifty-year-old Wych elm in Newcastle, Co Down has grown sideways owing to strong winds
The “astonishing and bizarre” Bendy Tree in Northern Ireland has been crowned the winner of this year’s tree of the year competition.
The wych elm tree, located in Newcastle, County Down, owes its name to its near horizontal trunk, which has grown sideways owing to the strong seaside winds coming off the Irish Sea.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Bendy elm still standing against all odds crowned UK tree of the year

articles.author: Andrew Roth Global affairs correspondent
articles.description:
In the shadow of the Parthenon, the secretary of state gave a selective reading of history as he urged Europe to ‘awaken from its slumber’
The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, delivered a classically inspired apologia for Donald Trump’s “America first” foreign policy on Wednesday, giving a sweeping speech to the backdrop of the Parthenon in Athens that appeared tailor-made for campaign ads if he runs for president in 2028.
In the speech, the top US diplomat drew historical parallels from the founders, philosophers and conquerers of antiquity to the modern American spirit – as well as his family’s own journey to the United States – as he called on Europe to “awaken from its long slumber” and reject a “future of atrophy and servitude and decline”.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Rubio in Greece digs into past to tout Trump’s ‘America first’ approach

articles.author: Nadeem Badshah
articles.description:
Ethan Scott Brown died after being wrongly told he would not be eligible to graduate from the University of Glasgow 
The family of a student who took his own life after being wrongly told he would not be eligible to graduate have said the University of Glasgow “will be held to account”.
Ethan Scott Brown, 23, was due to graduate in December 2024 after studying geography.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Family of student who took his own life say university ‘will be held to account’

articles.author: Seham Tantesh in Gaza and Jason Burke
articles.description:
People tell of lives changed beyond recognition after the 7 October attacks by Hamas three years ago and the subsequent Israeli offensive 


Ahmed Ishtaiwi has six chairs. They are cheap and plastic and battered, but they are among the 43-year-old driver and mechanic’s most valuable possessions.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘Neither war nor peace’: Palestinians in Gaza on existing amid disease, despair and ruins

articles.author: Ashifa Kassam and Sam Jones in Madrid
articles.description:
Maricarmen’s eviction from Madrid apartment after over seven decades set off wave of protests against housing crisis

‘Now is the moment’: housing activists at Madrid encampment pin wary hopes on Spain’s early election

María del Carmen Abascal, the 87-year-old whose eviction set off a nationwide wave of protests against Spain’s housing crisis, has died.
News of her death came two weeks after Maricarmen, as she had come to be known across Spain, was evicted from the Madrid apartment where she had lived for more than seven decades.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: María del Carmen Abascal, symbol of Spain’s housing protests, dies aged 87

articles.author: Luke Harding Senior international correspondent
articles.description:
‘Transparent information sharing’ from Moscow is required to conduct full risk assessment, UN agency says
The World Health Organization has said it does not have the “full picture” from Russia following the suspected death from plague last week of a 28-year-old laboratory worker in Siberia.
Darya Shipilova died two days after falling ill with cold-like symptoms. She was an employee at the anti-plague research institute in the eastern city of Irkutsk, with some reports suggesting she was infected after a workplace accident.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: WHO says it does not have ‘full picture’ from Russia following suspected plague death

articles.author: Ariana Baio
articles.description:
President floats firing Chris LaCivita and James Blair over any ‘conflict’ after reports of work in Republika Srpska
Donald Trump distanced himself from two top advisers on Wednesday, claiming he did not have “any idea who else they work for”, after it was reported they spent the weekend assisting a pro-Russia government in the Balkans.
On Truth Social, Trump wrote that Chris LaCivita, the co-manager of his 2024 presidential campaign, and James Blair, a campaign adviser and White House deputy chief of staff on leave of absence, “are outside consultants” and “do not work for me other than as outside consultants”.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Trump backs away from top aides who reportedly advised pro-Russia government

articles.author: Patrick Wintour Diplomatic editor
articles.description:
Group’s fighters hit key airport in Aden with explosive moments before plane from Cairo was due to land
Houthi forces appeared to be making slow advances on Wednesday in south-west Yemen, approaching the city of Taiz and firing a missile and an explosive towards the airport in Aden, the chief international hub of the Saudi-backed government.
The explosive hit the key airport moments before a plane was due to land. The British ambassador to Yemen, Abda Sharif, said the attack could have endangered thousands of people. It forced the flight – from Cairo – to be diverted to Jeddah and led to a review about the safety of flights in Aden.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Houthi forces appear to make slow advance in south-west Yemen

articles.author: Jonathan Watts
articles.description:
Inquest under way into why President Lula’s success in curbing Amazon deforestation has not led to success at polls 
More fire, more ash, more crime, more death. And a globally important ecosystem driven ever more rapidly towards a point of no return. That is the prospect for the Amazon rainforest for at least the next four years if Flávio Bolsonaro holds on to the lead he established this week in the first round of Brazil’s presidential election.
This appears to be of far more concern to the outside world than to voters in Latin America’s biggest, richest and most biodiverse nation.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Flávio Bolsonaro’s advance in Brazil’s election is grim jolt for climate campaigners

articles.author: Leyland Cecco in Toronto
articles.description:
Legislation is an effort by ruling Liberals to address growing clash over who has access to doctor-assisted death
Canada’s federal government said on Wednesday it would advance legislation to prevent people whose sole health condition is mental illness from accessing euthanasia, an effort by the ruling Liberal party to address a clash in the country over who has access to physician-assisted death.
Under the current rules, people whose sole underlying medical condition is a mental illness have been barred from accessing medical assistance in dying (Maid) to end their lives. But that ban – due to be lifted in March – has divided lawmakers over whether to permit this expansion of the Maid program.
In Canada, Crisis Services Canada can be contacted at any time on 1.833.456.4566, or via text on 45645 from 4pm-12am ET. In the US, you can call or text the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org. In the UK and Ireland, Samaritans can be contacted on freephone 116 123. In Australia, the crisis support service Lifeline is 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found at befrienders.org
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Canada to indefinitely bar mental illness as sole reason for access to euthanasia

articles.author: William Christou and Sufian Taha in Jerusalem
articles.description:
Forced closure marks low point in UK-Israeli relations, with reports UK is considering retaliatory expulsion of Israeli diplomats from London
The UK consulate in East Jerusalem gave few signs it was at the centre of a geopolitical controversy this week, with little movement around the high-walled building save the fluttering of the union jack and the occasional car exiting the compound.
The mission is to shut its doors on Thursday after Israel ordered its closure in response to a UK ban on trade with illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank and sanctions on those who help build or finance them.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘Palestinians will bear the cost’: UK consulate in East Jerusalem prepares to shut its doors

articles.author: Tom Phillips in Rio de Janeiro
articles.description:
After a surprise first-round victory, critics suggest son of disgraced ex-president could seek to continue his father’s authoritarian project

Flávio’s surprise first-round win highlights rapid rise of Brazil’s House of Bolsonaro

Flávio Bolsonaro, the far-right frontrunner to become Brazil’s next president, has vowed to “re-democratise” the South American country, increasing fears about a move into authoritarian rule if he wins power.
Brazil was re-democratised in the 1980s after a brutal 21-year dictatorship that Flávio’s father, the disgraced ex-president Jair Bolsonaro, has long praised.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘Another coup d’état’: fears grow as Flávio Bolsonaro vows to ‘re-democratise’ Brazil

articles.author: Oliver Holmes in Bangkok
articles.description:
New ‘support and training centre’ prompts concern in region but China says it is ‘not directed at any third party’ 
Satellite images show attack jets stationed at a new Chinese military facility in Laos, which opened last week and gives Beijing’s air force its first foothold in mainland south-east Asia.
Images provided by the commercial satellite provider Vantor show eight light attack aircraft positioned at Ban Keun airport alongside what appear to be more than a dozen military vehicles lined up in rows.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Satellite images show attack jets at Chinese military facility in Laos

articles.author: Martin Patriquin in Montreal
articles.description:
Lack of majority for Parti Québécois puts any referendum in doubt, especially amid bruising trade war with Trump
The victory of the Parti Québécois in Monday’s election in Quebec might seem to bring its signature goal, of separating the French-speaking province from Canada, much closer – but Canadian unity may not be nearly as threatened as may first seem.
The PQ’s victory was both impressive and disappointing. The party added 56 seats to its roster and more than doubled its vote share compared with the 2022 election, giving it its first taste of power in 14 years. Crucially, however, it was left five seats short of a majority, making its promise to hold a referendum after Donald Trump leaves office in 2028 nearly impossible.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Separatists win in Quebec – but does that bring separation from Canada any closer?

articles.author: Eva Corlett in Auckland and Adeshola Ore in Melbourne
articles.description:
Hamam al-Hammami spent 175 days in New Zealand until May 2019, as Australian Jewish group calls for full investigation into his time in Melbourne
New Zealand authorities have launched their own investigation into the flydubai co-pilot who allegedly tried to hijack an Israel-bound plane, after police confirmed he underwent flight training there about a year after he abandoned a degree in Australia.
Disaster was narrowly averted on 30 September when passengers and crew intervened to stop the alleged attempt of the co-pilot, Hamam al-Hammami, 29, to take control of a flight to Tel Aviv with 182 people onboard.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Flydubai attack investigation widens as alleged hijacker’s training in New Zealand scrutinised

articles.author: Keely Aouga
articles.description:
Justice department detained James Codey Bryant and allege he offered ‘technical advice’ to primary suspect
A surprise suspected accomplice has been arrested in connection with a mass school shooting in Canada that was made notorious after an 18-year-old allegedly killed six children after discussing it with the AI chatbot ChatGPT.
The US Department of Justice said on Tuesday it had detained James Codey Bryant, 30, a resident of western Washington state, on a charge of conspiracy to murder persons in a foreign country.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: US man arrested as second suspect in Canada mass school shooting planned with ChatGPT

articles.author: William Christou in Jerusalem and agencies
articles.description:
Jaafar Ashtiyeh was covering violence against olive farmers when settlers set upon him with the butts of their rifles 
Armed Israeli settlers beat a photographer in the presence of Israeli soldiers, hospitalising him, as he covered worsening settler violence against olive farmers in the occupied West Bank.
Jaafar Ashtiyeh, a 58-year-old veteran photographer for Agence France-Presse in Palestine, was assaulted by a group of settlers, who beat him with the butts of their rifles, despite him being marked as press. He was assaulted in view of about a dozen armed Israeli soldiers.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Israeli settlers beat press photographer as soldiers watch in West Bank

articles.author: Emma Graham-Harrison and Quique Kierszenbaum in Nir Oz
articles.description:
Israeli communities shattered by Hamas massacres are torn between rebuilding their lives and remembering lost friends and relatives
Keith Siegel spent many of his long hours in Hamas captivity in Gaza etching everything that happened after 7 October 2023 into his memory. For 484 days, he recited to himself every place he was held, the dates he was moved and every attack or humiliation he endured or witnessed.
He aimed to store intelligence that could help Israeli forces free other hostages if he was released, to keep track of time as the days slid by and be able to tell his family what happened to him. Now his body is free, but he cannot loosen those memories.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘All I want to do is cry’: trauma of 7 October survivors three years after the attacks

articles.author: Rachel Savage and agencies
articles.description:
Health minister says 28 contacts identified after death of citizen who arrived from DRC on Saturday
Kenya has reported its first-ever Ebola death, the health minister announced on Tuesday, as the disease continues to spread rapidly through the north-east of the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), where the outbreak was announced in May.
This is the 17th outbreak of the highly infectious, often deadly disease in the DRC. As of 2 October, 4,082 people had died out of 8,463 confirmed cases in the country since the emergence of the Bundibugyo strain of the Ebola virus, for which there is still no vaccine nor specific treatment.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Kenya confirms first Ebola case as virus ‘surges’ in DR Congo province

articles.author: Lucy Kassa
articles.description:
Civilians try to flee as men and boys rounded up on streets by new alliance as Ethiopia conflict erupts again
As renewed fighting has threatened a fresh humanitarian crisis in the northern region of Ethiopia, reports are emerging that a new alliance of armed groups in Tigray has been forcibly recruiting men and boys to its ranks.
Renewed conflict erupted on 23 September between Ethiopia’s federal government and the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), which rules the region, shattering the fragile Pretoria peace agreement signed between the two sides in November 2022.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Tigray rebel groups ‘forcibly recruiting boys as young as 15’ as fighting spreads

articles.author: Hannah Ellis-Petersen in Delhi
articles.description:
Pakistani authorities insist marchers calling for former PM to be released from jail will not reach the capital
Imran Khan’s supporters have begun a march to Islamabad to demand his release from jail after efforts by the government to halt the protest failed.
The march began in the former prime minister’s stronghold province of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa in north-west Pakistan on Sunday, according to leaders of his Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Supporters of Imran Khan start march on locked-down Islamabad

articles.author: Mohamed Gabobe in Mogadishu
articles.description:
After Guardian investigation uncovered drone strike that killed 12 civilians and injured many more, seven-year-old Abdiqadir Salah underwent vital operation in Mogadishu
On the rickshaw ride to the hospital, Marian Haji Abdi Guled felt a mixture of joy and apprehension: the day they had been waiting for had finally arrived.
Almost a year earlier, her then seven-year-old son, Abdiqadir Salah, had been seriously injured, alongside his two siblings, in what a Guardian investigation found was a US drone strike on the village of Jamaame in Somalia that killed at least 12 civilians, including eight children.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Guardian readers fund life-changing surgery for Somali boy injured in US airstrike

articles.author: Nicola Davis Science correspondent
articles.description:
Study of remains taken from royal cemetery at Umm el-Qa’ab appears to confirm early Egyptologist’s theory
Court officials and craftspeople serving early Egyptian kings may have been sacrificed when their ruler died, according to research that found fractures in several ancient skulls.
The royal cemetery of Umm el-Qa’ab near Abydos features the tombs and enclosures of the First Dynasty rulers of Egypt, and dates as far back as 3,000BC.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Skull fractures suggest servants of Egypt’s ancient kings were sacrificed

articles.author: William Christou in Jerusalem
articles.description:
Calls for release of six Matsadaash staff after one is charged, while whereabouts of other five remain unknown
An Egyptian journalist has been charged with joining a terrorist group, days after an entire newsroom was detained in what rights groups have said is a crackdown on press freedoms.
Last week, authorities arrested six journalists from the independent fact-checking and investigative platform Matsadaash – literally meaning “don’t believe” – accusing them in a statement of being unlicensed and publishing false news on behalf of the outlawed Muslim Brotherhood.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Egyptian journalist faces terrorism charges after entire newsroom detained

articles.author: Hannah Ellis-Petersen in Mumbai
articles.description:
Thousands gather in Mumbai with heavy police presence as concerns mount that millions will be denied voting rights
India’s youth-led Cockroach movement kicked off more nationwide protests on Friday as thousands of people gathered in Mumbai, amid mounting concerns that millions of citizens are being unfairly stripped of their vote.
The movement, which calls itself the Cockroach Janta party (CJP) and has massive support among the country’s gen Zs, returned to the streets to demand the resignation of the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: India’s Cockroach movement launches new protests over changes to voter roll

articles.author: Megan Davies and James Michelin for MetDesk
articles.description:
Up to 300mm of rain could fall in places, while extreme downpours bring landslides and deaths in Nepal
Torrential rain and potentially damaging flooding are forecast in eastern Spain over the coming days, as cold upper air moves over the warm, humid surface air of the Mediterranean Sea, fuelling violent, slow-moving thunderstorms near Spain’s east coast. The weather pattern, known as a Dana, occurs most often in autumn.
Models show more than 100mm of rain could fall across the region on Friday, with 200-300mm possible in some areas. Cities including Valencia and Castelló de la Plana, are most at risk. Valencia has experienced several damaging floods in recent years. Catalonia has now put three towns under lockdown and Valencia has shut schools for nearly half a million children.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Eastern Spain braces for torrential rain and flooding

articles.author: William Christou
articles.description:
Smit Machchhar says in video call with Indian PM that he realised if he did not get up ‘passengers would lose their lives’
The Indian pilot who helped thwart an apparent attempt to crash a flydubai flight to Tel Aviv said his faith and his desire to save his passengers allowed him to make a “last push” to open the cockpit door as he fought for his life.
Capt Smit Machchhar, who was recovering in an Abu Dhabi hospital, described to India’s prime minister, Narendra Modi, how he helped save the plane and its more than 170 passengers.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘I was fighting for my life’: Indian pilot hailed as hero recalls flydubai cockpit attack

articles.author: Patrick Wintour Diplomatic editor
articles.description:
Indian government issued with warning it would be in contempt of court if it failed to release Jagtar Singh Johal
The British Sikh activist Jagtar Singh Johal has been released from a Delhi prison after the Indian high court warned the government it would be found in contempt of court if it continued to attempt to keep him in jail despite an 18 September court order releasing him on bail. Johal has been incarcerated for nine years without any full trial.
The court order was issued after Johal’s lawyers issued a writ of habeas corpus alleging he was being detained against the express direction of the court.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: British Sikh activist released from Delhi jail after nine-year detention

articles.author: David Smith in Washington
articles.description:
Trump briefly stepped away from the microphone after one protester appeared to approach the stage
Donald Trump’s latest campaign rally was rocked by repeated protests on Wednesday as the US president urged Texas voters to back embattled Senate candidate Ken Paxton.
At least half a dozen demonstrators interrupted the US president during his remarks in San Antonio, with some led away by police. One was physically assaulted by an older Trump supporter as he tried to leave the arena.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Donald Trump’s Texas rally rocked by repeated protests

articles.author: Robert Mackey, Shrai Popat, Marina Dunbar and Tom Ambrose
articles.description:
This live blog is now closed.

Sign up for the Breaking News US email

Tonight, we’ll have another set of midterm debates. In Iowa, we’ll see the Republican nominee for US Senate, Ashley Hinson, face off against Democrat Josh Turek, a state representative and Paralympian at 8pm ET.
The race has become one of the most competitive of this cycle, despite the fact a Democrat hasn’t won a Senate election in the Hawkeye state since 2008. Turek, however, trails by just a point in a recent New York Times/Siena College poll. And Hinson, who currently serves as a congresswoman, has pushed back on Donald Trump’s agenda of late, as the president’s approval rating sinks to a new low. Hinson has called for an end on the war in Iran, despite consistently voting against House war powers resolutions that would curb military action, and criticizing the president’s recent pause on tariffs for foreign beef imports, which, Hinson argues, will affect the bottom line for the many cattle ranchers in Iowa.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Trump repeats his false claim that Iran could destroy Los Angeles or San Diego – as it happened

articles.author: Stephanie Kirchgaessner
articles.description:
Jamie Raskin says ‘startling’ email asked whether young woman was ‘for me, or are you keeping her for yourself’
A powerful Democratic lawmaker has called for a criminal investigation into former Bard College president Leon Botstein after congressional investigators uncovered an email from Botstein to accused sex trafficker Jeffrey Epstein in which he says Botstein asked if a young woman was “for me, or are you keeping her for yourself”.
The latest development appears to have triggered the immediate resignation of Botstein from all Bard-affiliated positions, including his professorship and roles in Bard’s music programs. Botstein had led the college for 50 years and only recently stepped down as president.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Leon Botstein resigns from Bard roles as key Democrat demands investigation into Epstein links

articles.author: Robert Mackey
articles.description:
Ads promoting the president have cost more than $12m and his Super Pac has refused to reimburse taxpayers

Sign up to The Stakes 2026: your weekly guide to the US midterms

The Democratic National Committee sued the Trump administration in federal court on Wednesday, asking a judge in Washington DC to stop the president from using taxpayer funds to air a series of ads promoting himself, arguing that the ads are illegal government-sponsored propaganda.
The ads promoting Donald Trump, including one recycled from his 2024 presidential campaign, have cost taxpayers more than $12m so far, according to the media tracking firm AdImpact.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Democrats sue to stop Trump from using taxpayer funds for self-promoting ads

articles.author: Ariana Baio
articles.description:
President floats firing Chris LaCivita and James Blair over any ‘conflict’ after reports of work in Republika Srpska
Donald Trump distanced himself from two top advisers on Wednesday, claiming he did not have “any idea who else they work for”, after it was reported they spent the weekend assisting a pro-Russia government in the Balkans.
On Truth Social, Trump wrote that Chris LaCivita, the co-manager of his 2024 presidential campaign, and James Blair, a campaign adviser and White House deputy chief of staff on leave of absence, “are outside consultants” and “do not work for me other than as outside consultants”.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Trump backs away from top aides who reportedly advised pro-Russia government

articles.author: Editorial
articles.description:
Donald Trump’s unpopularity and the economic struggles of voters have boosted Democrats. But with less than a month to go, there is no complacency
For once, Democrats and Donald Trump might be in agreement: “Pretend I’m on the ticket,” the historically unpopular president has instructed supporters. Midterms are in large part a referendum on the incumbent, and Trump’s war on Iran and its impact on the cost of living have boosted support for Democrats. With less than a month to go, they have reason to be upbeat. The party has a mountain to climb after the devastating defeats of 2024, and the gerrymandering of Republicans, but surveys give it a lead of about nine points on the generic ballot, which measures preference for parties rather than specific candidates.
Attention has turned from the prospects of seizing the House, where Democrats are forecast a clear majority, to what once seemed like the highly optimistic possibility of taking the Senate too. That would require flipping four seats, with 35 in play. Remarkably, Democrats are prospering in red states from Texas to Alaska. In Kansas – which Mr Trump carried by 16 points, and which has not elected a Democratic senator since 1932 – the race is neck and neck.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: The Guardian view on the US midterms: the cost of living is on the ballot, but this is about democracy too | Editorial

articles.author: Chris Stein, Alex Clark, Andrew Witherspoon and Ashley Kirk
articles.description:
These graphics explain what the Democrats would need to do to flip the Senate and House of Representatives
A turning point in Donald Trump’s second term will soon arrive. On 3 November, voters across the US will decide whether to keep the president’s Republican allies in control of Congress, or return Democrats to the majority.
Many indicators of voter sentiment suggest the Democrats are favored to take back control of the House of Representatives, and potentially the Senate. Winning either would be a significant victory for the party and give it the power to block Trump’s legislative agenda and more aggressively investigate his administration.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: The US midterm races that will decide control of Congress – mapped

articles.author: Ted Widmer
articles.description:
We appear to be entering a new era, in which political desperation at home leads to increasingly unhinged threats abroad
Donald Trump was in Nebraska on Monday, and though his long rally speech had elements of a performance, this was no Bruce Springsteen album. He offered another dark meditation on a world spiraling out of control, one in which the destruction of American cities is increasingly a possibility, unless Americans trust him to use the vast powers of the presidency to annihilate his foes.
The president drew fury when he suggested that Iran could launch a nuclear attack and “take out” Los Angeles or San Diego. California leaders reacted with scorn at Trump’s alarmism.
Ted Widmer, a former White House speechwriter, is the editor of American Speeches, and the recently published The Living Declaration: A Biography of America’s Founding Text, both published by the Library of America
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘Take out’ Los Angeles and San Diego? Trump is beyond irresponsible | Ted Widmer

articles.author: Marilyn W Thompson
articles.description:
Sir James Goldsmith’s links to Hilton Head, South Carolina, add to mystery of Jane Doe 4, who claimed she was abused by Epstein in the 1980s
For Jeffrey Epstein, the billionaire Goldsmith family was a gateway to elite society and he wanted to be in their circle.
The disgraced financier, who died in prison in 2019 facing sex-trafficking charges, longed for a billionaire’s lifestyle and cultivated the family’s friends, bankers, business associates and advisers.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: British billionaire warned Epstein was a ‘sexual deviant’ decades before FBI closed in on the abuser

articles.author: Laure Boulinier, Sofia Couceiro and Boglarka Kosztolanyi
articles.description:
The US midterms may not be as much of a spectacle as the presidential elections, but they are just as important and can completely change not just the course of a presidential term, but federal legislation for years to come. The Guardian unpacks how these elections work, what the results mean and how they affect American life
 Continue reading...
articles.title: US midterms: what are they and why do presidents dread them? – explainer

articles.author: Akin Olla
articles.description:
There’s an unsung reason for the organization’s success even as other leftwing groups face a bumpy road
A lot has been written recently in an effort to understand the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) and how we’ve risen to such prominence in a short time.
It is clear that we reflect a growing disillusionment with the Democratic party, and a further radicalization of the American population. But many leftwing social movement organizations, such as Black Lives Matter and the Women’s March, have risen in the last decade or so, and many groups, from MoveOn to the Sunrise Movement, have attempted to absorb large numbers of people, influence the Democratic party and enter the public consciousness with lower levels of success.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Why are the Democratic Socialists of America so successful? | Akin Olla

articles.author: Michael Sainato
articles.description:
The project has sparked doubts over whether the plant will be built and delivered as promised, given Trump’s record
Donald Trump has long sought to portray himself as a man of steel, from the White House photoshopping Trump to look like Superman, to enacting tariffs on steel and approving the sale of US Steel to Japan’s Nippon Steel with a ”golden” share given to the US government.
Most recently, the Trump administration announced plans to construct the largest steel plant in the US, a $15bn plant in Lee county, Iowa, to be built by India-based Mesabi Metallics.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Skepticism mires Trump’s Iowa steel plant project: ‘Promises are not the same as jobs’

articles.author: Arwa Mahdawi
articles.description:
Having seemingly written off the midterms, the Republican bigwigs are making their pitches for 2028. But the current commander-in-chief could be looking closer to home
The US midterm elections are a month away and it’s looking rough for the Republicans. I wouldn’t discount devious schemes behind the scenes, but, on the face of it, the president and his entourage seem to be flailing. Donald Trump is desperately dangling money in front of voters and promising “a big surprise”. Meanwhile, the vice-president, JD Vance, and the GOP senator Ted Cruz seem more concerned with fighting over who will be Trump’s heir than with the midterms.
If the polls are to be believed, Vance is the frontrunner for the Republican presidential nomination in 2028. But while he may have great name recognition, Vance is also unlikable. According to the CNN analyst Harry Enten, he is one of the least popular vice-presidents in history. He’s also apparently made enemies within his own party, largely because of his scepticism about the Iran war. His detractors include Cruz, who told MS Now in August that Vance wasn’t a shoo-in for the nomination. The party, Cruz said, was still figuring out the best candidate and needed “to decide who we are, what do we believe”.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: JD Vance and Ted Cruz are fighting for control of the GOP. The problem? Neither is called Trump | Arwa Mahdawi

articles.author: Timothy Pratt
articles.description:
NSPM-7 Defendants Union plans to offer legal clinics, media training and more to people facing prosecution for protest
Darío Sánchez is facing state charges related to a protest he did not attend. Indictments against the 33-year-old Texas middle school teacher have changed three times. He has also been arrested and released three times, most recently for an online search for how to replace an old Game Boy battery; police alleged he was seeking information on explosives.
“I’ve seen my case as one manifestation of all the different ways the Trump administration is going after people – regardless of if you’ve even been to a protest,” Sánchez said. “The reality is, as long as you disagree with the government, you’re a target.”
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Trump 2.0 is targeting US protesters with ‘antifa’ charges. Activists started a union to fight back

articles.author: Presented by Jonathan Freedland with James Henson, produced by Nada Smiljanic and Danielle Stephens
articles.description:
Democratic Senate nominee James Talarico is surprising everyone, as polls have him leading his Republican opponent, Ken Paxton, in the Republican-led state of Texas.

Jonathan Freedland speaks to James Henson, founder and executive director of the Texas Politics Project, about why a blue wave in the Lone Star state would be seismic
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Is James Talarico about to flip Texas for the Democrats? | Politics Weekly America

articles.author: Presented by Lucy Hough with Clive Stafford Smith ; produced by Angus Neale ; senior producer Ryan Ramgobin ; executive producer Zoe Hitch
articles.description:
A woman convicted of murdering a schoolmate 30 years ago has been taken to hospital after surviving two rounds of lethal injections in Tennessee. Christa Pike would have been the first woman to be executed in the state in 200 years. Pike, 50, has spent three decades on death row after she was convicted of the murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer in 1995. A last-minute appeal to stop the lethal injection was overturned by the supreme court, but the state governor, Bill Lee, has suspended executions in Tennessee for the rest of the year. Lucy Hough speaks to the attorney and anti-capital punishment campaigner Clive Stafford Smith – watch on YouTube
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Death row inmate Christa Pike survives two lethal injections in Tennessee - The Latest

articles.author: Tom Phillips, Bryony Moore, Karif Wat and Boglarka Kosztolanyi
articles.description:
Brazil will head to the polls on 4 October for the first vote in its presidential race. The incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, is neck-and-neck with Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of the former president Jair Bolsonaro, who is in prison for plotting a military coup. There are fears and accusations that the US is interfering in the election, and these follow similar allegations in a string of elections across Latin America won by Donald Trump-backed candidates in what is being called 'the orange wave'.
The Guardian's Latin America correspondent, Tom Phillips, explains the tactics Trump and his administration have been using in recent months and what impact another Bolsonaro government could have on the region, and the world
 Continue reading...
articles.title: How Trump is meddling in Brazil's election – explainer

articles.author: Jillian Ambrose Energy correspondent
articles.description:
Move expected to make pump pricing more transparent and encourage competition after diesel hits record £2 a litre
Drivers will be able to see live petrol prices on Google Maps for the first time from Thursday, in a move that will help motorists shop around for the cheapest fuel.
Millions of motorists will be able to find the cheapest petrol and diesel prices by searching for a local forecourt in the Google app, in what could prove to be “a major development” in making fuel prices more fair, according to campaigners.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: UK motorists can now see live fuel prices on Google Maps

articles.author: Ben Quinn with photographs by Graeme Robertson
articles.description:
Little if any sign Bury Park is a place where any group might fear to tread, despite Tory MP’s comments to the contrary
From behind the counter of his chippie, Tanner Ahmed is wrestling with the notion that the regular stop-off point for fans attending Luton Town’s nearby football ground could be in a “no-go zone” for white people.
“The whole point of setting up was to cater for thousands who were coming through here every week, especially in the first year when the club was in the Premier League,” said Ahmed, affectionately known as Mr T, in the Bury Park area, a predominantly Asian district of Luton.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘I feel perfectly safe’: white Lutonians on the town’s supposed no-go zones

articles.author: Nicola Chester
articles.description:
Linkenholt, Hampshire and Wexcombe, Wiltshire: Even to the untrained eye, traditional ones and modern, regenerative ones look very different
Stubble fields, those post-harvest acres of short straws, seem to be lasting longer into the season, as farmers respond to changing practices. I have a wistful attachment to stubble fields: for so long a kind of temporary commons where, for a few redundant weeks before autumn or winter ploughing, you could shortcut across them, the dew-filled straws flicking water up the inside of your legs. But today, stubble fields aren’t all equal.
Below Cleve Hill Down, a tractor is drilling winter wheat directly into bare seedbed between the stubble. Regularly sprayed with herbicide, it is free of weeds or any green – a pale-gold spread of machine-knitted tweed. A hundred years ago, the stubble would be left, full of weeds, birds and insects, until midwinter ploughing, allowing frosts to break down the clods.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Country diary: The changing face of stubble fields, those shortcuts of my youth | Nicola Chester

articles.author: Andrew Gregory Health editor
articles.description:
Operation on 19-year-old who had no sperm after chemotherapy offers hope of preserving children’s fertility after cancer treatment 
Surgeons have performed the first testicular tissue transplant on a teenager in the UK, offering hope that boys left infertile by chemotherapy could one day have biological children.
The 19-year-old had his tissue removed and frozen three years ago before undergoing treatment for a serious blood disorder. He said he was “incredibly grateful” to the medical team behind the pioneering procedure, which represents a potential breakthrough for male fertility preservation.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Teenager becomes first person to have testicular tissue transplant in UK

articles.author: Pippa Neill Environment reporter
articles.description:
Hundred-and-fifty-year-old Wych elm in Newcastle, Co Down has grown sideways owing to strong winds
The “astonishing and bizarre” Bendy Tree in Northern Ireland has been crowned the winner of this year’s tree of the year competition.
The wych elm tree, located in Newcastle, County Down, owes its name to its near horizontal trunk, which has grown sideways owing to the strong seaside winds coming off the Irish Sea.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Bendy elm still standing against all odds crowned UK tree of the year

articles.author: Nadeem Badshah
articles.description:
Ethan Scott Brown died after being wrongly told he would not be eligible to graduate from the University of Glasgow 
The family of a student who took his own life after being wrongly told he would not be eligible to graduate have said the University of Glasgow “will be held to account”.
Ethan Scott Brown, 23, was due to graduate in December 2024 after studying geography.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Family of student who took his own life say university ‘will be held to account’

articles.author: Richard Adams Education editor
articles.description:
Overhaul of special education in England could unravel, thinktank finds, because of ‘use it before you lose it’ dynamic
Labour’s flagship changes to special education in England are at risk of unravelling because parents are rushing to secure support for their children before the system changes, new analysis has found.
The Institute for Government (IfG) thinktank says the government’s plans to largely replace education, health and care plans (EHCPs) in England with more widespread support in mainstream schools may be too optimistic and take longer to complete than its 2030 timeline.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Labour Send changes at risk as parents rush to secure support, say experts

articles.author: Rajeev Syal Home affairs editor
articles.description:
Convicted pair, plus third man released in August, have IPPs replaced after serving much longer than minimum terms
Two men jailed with indefinite sentences for public protection (IPPs) have been freed after each serving about two decades in custody despite receiving minimum terms of two years or less.
A high court judge and a magistrate hearing an appeal after a review by the Criminal Cases Review Commission (CCRC) told Luke Ings and Liam Bennett they would be freed, and also replaced an indeterminate sentence given to a third man, James Ward.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Two men serving indefinite jail sentences freed after two decades

articles.author: Pippa Crerar Political editor
articles.description:
Party hopes to win over affluent middle-class voters as leader rejects calls to ‘unite the right’ in conference speech

Kemi Badenoch has announced that the Conservatives would abolish inheritance tax on family homes if elected, prompting criticism that she is prioritising cutting taxes for the rich.
The Tory leader also said couples would be able to leave an additional tax-free sum of £1m to their families, as the party attempts to shore up its traditional base in southern England.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Tories accused of prioritising rich voters as Badenoch lays out inheritance tax cut plan

articles.author: Chris Osuh
articles.description:
Organisations honour those who died three years ago as Andy Burnham says government stands with British Jews
British Jewish organisations gathered in central London on Wednesday for a vigil honouring victims of the 7 October attacks in Israel, after a day of tributes from politicians and community leaders.
The vigil took place at Richmond Terrace, opposite Downing Street. The Board of Deputies of British Jews said: “Three years ago, Hamas terrorists infiltrated Israel, murdering 1,200 men, women and children, injuring thousands and taking 251 people captive. May their memories for ever remain a blessing.”
 Continue reading...
articles.title: British Jewish groups hold London vigil for victims of 7 October attacks

articles.description:
Conservative leader condemns Reform UK for suggesting black people cannot be English in her speech at the Tory party conference in Birmingham on Wednesday. While she acknowledges many Reform supporters are 'our people' who have been let down by the party, she says they deserve better than Reform politicians


Tories accused of prioritising rich voters as Badenoch lays out inheritance tax cut plan

UK politics live – as it happened

 Continue reading...
articles.title: Kemi Badenoch condemns Reform UK in Conservative conference speech – video

articles.author: Heather Stewart Economics editor
articles.description:
The Tory leader’s proposal to slash the tax would shovel £6bn of taxpayer money to the already-wealthy
Kemi Badenoch’s inheritance tax gambit is a Conservative classic. After all, it was George Osborne’s high-profile pledge to “take the family home out of inheritance tax” in 2007 that put Gordon Brown off calling a snap general election.
In practice, Osborne’s plan involved a £1m threshold for inheritance tax – and given the global financial crisis had blown a hole in the public finances by the time the Conservative-Lib Dem coalition came to power in 2010, it never came to pass.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Badenoch’s inheritance tax gambit makes no economic sense | Heather Stewart

articles.author: Rowena Mason Whitehall editor
articles.description:
Internal inquiry exonerates Dan Jukes and James Orr, who were filmed talking about scheme involving US donor
Reform UK has cleared two of its senior officials of breaking laws that ban foreign donations, despite the matter remaining under police investigation.
The party published a 27-page report of an internal inquiry finding that Dan Jukes, Nigel Farage’s press adviser, and James Orr, its head of policy, had not breached funding rules.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Reform clears its own officials of breaking party funding laws despite police investigation

articles.author: Guardian Staff
articles.description:
Readers respond to an article in which Larry Elliott argues that Andy Burnham must challenge neoliberal nostrums
Larry Elliott’s column on the rightwing economic myths constraining Andy Burnham’s government should be required reading before John Healey’s budget (Rightwing economic myths could derail Burnham’s project – to destroy them, look to Keynes, 1 October).
I spent 20 years trading bonds, and agree that the household budget analogy bears no relation to how the UK state finances itself. Parliament votes on the spending, the Treasury instructs the Bank of England, and the Bank credits accounts in the private sector. Taxes withdraw money afterwards.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Beware rightwing economic myths such as ‘maxing out the nation’s credit card’ | Letters

articles.author: Heather Stewart and Jessica Elgot
articles.description:
Energy and housing costs threaten biggest decline in modern times unless bold action taken, says thinktank
Soaring energy and housing costs mean Labour is on course to preside over the worst parliament for living standards in modern times, a stark analysis warns.
Three weeks ahead of John Healey’s budget, the Joseph Rowntree Foundation said Britain faces a “dire” outlook unless the government takes “bold policy action”.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Labour could oversee worst parliament on record for living standards, study warns

articles.author: Joanna Partridge
articles.description:
Acquittals of five former bankers come year after supreme court overturned ruling against City trader Tom Hayes
Five more former traders who were jailed for rigging interest rates have had their convictions quashed by the court of appeal in London, after a long battle to clear their names.
The court overturned the convictions of Jay Vijay Merchant, Jonathan Mathew, Philippe Moryoussef, Alex Pabon and Colin Bermingham – all of whom worked at Barclays.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Ex-Barclays traders jailed for rigging interest rates have convictions quashed

articles.author: William Christou and Sufian Taha in Jerusalem
articles.description:
Forced closure marks low point in UK-Israeli relations, with reports UK is considering retaliatory expulsion of Israeli diplomats from London
The UK consulate in East Jerusalem gave few signs it was at the centre of a geopolitical controversy this week, with little movement around the high-walled building save the fluttering of the union jack and the occasional car exiting the compound.
The mission is to shut its doors on Thursday after Israel ordered its closure in response to a UK ban on trade with illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank and sanctions on those who help build or finance them.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘Palestinians will bear the cost’: UK consulate in East Jerusalem prepares to shut its doors

articles.author: Sarah Butler
articles.description:
Former Selfridges owners buy UK high street institution from long-term backer Stefano Pessina
The Canadian family that once owned Selfridges department store has bought the UK pharmacy and beauty retailer Boots for $8.9bn (£6.74bn).
Wittington Investments, the holding company of the Weston family that controls the Loblaws grocery chain and Shoppers Drug Mart pharmacy outlets in Canada, will own Boots’ UK and Irish retail operations and opticians chain, the No7 beauty brand and a franchise arm in Thailand.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Canada’s Weston family buys Boots for $8.9bn

articles.author: Peter Walker, Pippa Crerar, Rowena Mason and Jessica Elgot
articles.description:
At Conservative conference, some worry about becoming a one-woman party, while others say party should thank their lucky stars they have her
Kemi Badenoch has long said that the Conservatives were “under new management”, but in a TV interview to mark the end of a party conference at which she has been front and centre of more or less everything, she took the analogy further.
“Your viewers will know that sometimes you have a football team that’s disappointing,” the Tory leader told GB News. “There’s a new captain, there’s a new coach, there’s a new owner, effectively – which is all me.”
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘People are scared of her, to be honest’: Kemi Badenoch remakes Tories in her image

articles.author: Dan Sabbagh
articles.description:
Veteran leftwinger has been ‘in exile in the east’ in Russia and not been to Holborn and St Pancras constituency since campaign began
George Galloway has been elected seven times to parliament, but his attempt to succeed for an eighth this week, in the London seat formerly held by Keir Starmer, is undoubtedly his most curious effort yet.
Since the byelection campaign began, the leader of the Workers party of Britain has yet to set foot in the UK, let alone the Holborn and St Pancras constituency, because he is in what he describes as “self-exile” after being questioned by counter-terrorism police at Gatwick airport a year ago.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: George Galloway contests London byelection without setting foot in UK

articles.author: Eve Livingston
articles.description:
Scots-written Till the Bells Ring  premiered a year before the Hollywood film, which featured spoken words by Al Jolson
For almost a century, The Jazz Singer has been celebrated as the world’s first feature-length film to include synchronised dialogue (known as a “talkie”), and English as the first language of cinema. But a chance discovery threatens to upend film history with the news that it may have been beaten to the title by a full year – and by a film made in Glasgow and written in Scots.
The breakthrough was made by the historian and self-confessed “film nerd” Marc David Jacobs, who was conducting research for a book on the first wave of British sound films when he came across the story of Till the Bells Ring.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Scottish film could steal The Jazz Singer’s crown as ‘world’s first talkie’

articles.author: Matthew Taylor
articles.description:
‘Techno-optimism’ may lead to reliance on unproven solutions at expense of societal changes needed
Scientists who believe technology will largely solve the problems caused by the climate crisis are less likely to engage in civic action on the issue, according to a study.
The report from the London School of Economics found they are 23% less likelyto sign petitions or take part in protests than peers who doubt that technology is the answer. They are also 18% less likely to make high-impact lifestyle changes, from reducing flights to changing to a vegan or vegetarian diet.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Scientists who put faith in technology less likely to take climate action

articles.author: Patrick Barkham
articles.description:
Teenagers Eva Wishart and Emily Smith launch project to breed and release 250 of the tiny animals by September
Children in Devon are being invited to become “citizen captive breeders”, rearing harvest mice at home for release into the wild to help revive endangered nature.
Wild Pets, a new conservation project launched by two 14-year-old friends, is seeking 20 Devon-based children to rear hundreds of mice after the duo’s own successful restoration efforts.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Wanted: children to rear harvest mice at home for wild release in Devon

articles.author: Andrew Gregory Health editor
articles.description:
More than 1 million people in Great Britain now vape despite having never regularly smoked, ONS data shows
More than 1 million people in Great Britain now vape despite never having been regular smokers, with rates nearly doubling in just four years, according to figures that health experts describe as concerning.
About 5.4 million people aged 16 and above in England, Scotland and Wales (9.9%) used e-cigarettes daily or occasionally in 2025, Office for National Statistics data showed. Vaping was highest among those aged 25-34 (16.4%).
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Proportion of people in Great Britain vaping who never smoked doubles in four years

articles.author: Pippa Neill Environment reporter
articles.description:
Exclusive: Campaign group’s analysis of North Yorkshire plans finds datacentre would have to burn 4.9m tonnes of wood a year
Drax’s planned datacentre could produce nearly double the emissions of all flights out of Gatwick airport each year by burning 4.9m tonnes of wood annually, an analysis has shown.

articles.description:
There’s no Leon, Claire or Ada Wong in Cregger’s adaptation. Instead, it re-creates something more fundamental – the strange, terrifying experience of actually playing the game
• Don’t get Pushing Buttons delivered to your inbox? Sign up here
I’ve been surprised by the number of Resident Evil fans complaining on social media about Zach Cregger’s cinematic adaptation of the survival horror series. “It’s not a real Resident Evil movie,” they’ve claimed. Were we watching the same film? Certainly, it doesn’t feature any of the familiar heroes – there’s no Leon, no Claire, no Ada Wong – and there’s a distinct lack of recognisable antagonists and well-known locations. Despite all of this, Cregger’s interpretation is one of the most accurate and interesting video game films ever made.
On the surface, it’s about a zombifying virus that gets accidentally released in Raccoon City by the Umbrella Corporation. These are, of course, the foundations of the Resi mythos. More interestingly, Cregger seeks to replicate and explore the structural and narrative conventions of the series. In the film, the player character, hapless courier Bryan Hodukavich, is thrust into a viral outbreak, with no weapons and no idea what’s going on. He is then submerged into an uncanny shadow world of escalating peril and body horror. The film takes us through a series of locations dragged straight from the games – an abandoned farmhouse, a road tunnel crammed with abandoned cars, a hospital and the obligatory sewer level.
